svg.text: the premise and the psychology, in one book (1886)
BGE 36, steps 1 and 6
our drives are the only reality "given"
belief in the will's causality "is really
just our belief in causality itself"
so: posit will as the only causality,
and read the world "from inside" as will
a simple will that is known and that acts
is what the argument starts from
denies
BGE 16, 19, 34, twenty sections earlier
no "immediate certainties": not "I think",
not "I will" (16, 34)
willing is "something complicated,
something unified only in a word" (19)
philosophers "speak of the will as if it
were the best-known thing in the world" (19)
a simple will is what the psychology dissolved
the conclusion's term, a simple will that acts and that the world is made of, is supplied by
a premise the same book's psychology has taken apart: the argument assumes what it sets out
to prove, and its author frames every step but one as a supposition (Clark 1990, pp. 213–217)
